hints: Think about how many reactant molecules you start with and how many product molecules you finish with in an addition across a C=C bond.
walkthrough:
Picture what addition means**
Think of ethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$. It has a C=C double bond. In addition, something adds across that double bond and the double bond becomes a single bond. Nothing is lost or split off, everything joins together.
Final answer: An addition reaction is one in which two or more reactants combine to form only a single product.

hints: Recall what happens when chlorine dissolves in water, the same equilibrium that gives swimming pool water its disinfectant.
walkthrough:
Link chlorine and water**
You do not need a complex apparatus here. When chlorine gas is bubbled into or mixed with water it reacts reversibly with the water itself. One product is $\text{HCl}$ and the other is chloric(I) acid, $\text{HOCl}$.
Final answer: Mix $\text{Cl}_2$ with / dissolve $\text{Cl}_2$ in water: $\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HCl} + \text{HOCl}$

hints: Think where the $\text{Cl}_2$ / $\text{HOCl}$ equilibrium in water is most useful in everyday life for keeping water safe.
walkthrough:
Remember why HOCl matters**
$\text{HOCl}$ is a powerful oxidising and antibacterial agent. That is exactly why chlorine is added to drinking water and swimming pools. The $\text{HOCl}$ formed kills bacteria and other microbes, making the water safe.
Final answer: Water purification / disinfection by killing bacteria or microbes.

hints: Start with the polarity given as $\text{HO}^{\delta-}-\text{Cl}^{\delta+}$ and decide which atom the electron rich C=C double bond will attack.
Recall the first step of any electrophilic addition, the pi bond acts as a nucleophile and the X-Y bond breaks heterolytically to give an anion.
Think about what cation is left on carbon after $\text{Cl}$ has bonded to one carbon of ethene, and what anion is released.
Consider how the released $:\text{OH}^{-}$ ion with its lone pair then behaves toward the positively charged carbon.
walkthrough:
Spot the electrophile**
Look at $\text{HO}^{\delta-}-\text{Cl}^{\delta+}$. Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so chlorine carries the partial positive charge. That $\text{Cl}^{\delta+}$ is electron poor, so it is the electrophile. The C=C double bond in ethene is electron rich and will attack it.

Make the first bond and release hydroxide**
Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the $\text{C=C}$ double bond and pointing to the $\text{Cl}^{\delta+}$ atom. At the same time, draw a curly arrow from the $\text{HO-Cl}$ bond onto the O atom. The $\text{HO-Cl}$ bond breaks heterolytically to give $:\text{OH}^{-}$ with a full lone pair and a new C-Cl bond. The other carbon is left electron deficient.

Draw the carbocation intermediate**
After step 2 you have $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH}_2^{+}$. One carbon now bonded to $\text{Cl}$, the other carbon carries a full positive charge, a carbocation. Show the + charge on carbon and complete octets on $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ with lone pairs.

Attack by hydroxide to finish**
The $:\text{OH}^{-}$ ion is a nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on the O of $:\text{OH}^{-}$ directly to the positively charged carbon of the carbocation. This forms the C-O bond and gives the final product $\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}$ with no charges left.

Final answer: Curly arrow from $\text{HO-Cl}$ bond to O to form $\text{OH}^{-}$; curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{Cl}^{\delta+}$; intermediate $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH}_2^{+}$; curly arrow from lone pair on $:\text{OH}^{-}$ to carbocation C to give $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$.

hints: Focus on the change from $\text{-CH}_2\text{Cl}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{CN}$, what nucleophile replaces $\text{Cl}$ and what solvent favours substitution over hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Recognise chain extension by CN**
Step 1 converts $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ to $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$. This is nucleophilic substitution of $\text{Cl}$ by $\text{CN}^{-}$. The standard source of $\text{CN}^{-}$ is potassium cyanide, $\text{KCN}$, dissolved in ethanol with heating to favour substitution.

hints: Recall the named reaction that converts a $\text{-CN}$ group into a $\text{-COOH}$ group when heated with aqueous acid.
walkthrough:
Name the nitrile to acid change**
Step 2 converts $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ to $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ using $\text{HCl(aq)}$. The $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ group is hydrolysed by water in acid to a carboxylic acid group. This reaction type is acid hydrolysis.

hints: Remember that acid hydrolysis of a nitrile needs two molecules of water and produces the carboxylic acid plus an ammonium salt when $\text{HCl}$ is present.
walkthrough:
Balance atoms and account for ammonia**
Hydrolysis adds water across the $\text{-CN}$ group: $$\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$$ The nitrogen ends up as $\text{NH}_3$ which in $\text{HCl(aq)}$ is protonated to $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$. Check atoms: two waters supply the two O atoms for $\text{COOH}$ and the H atoms for $\text{NH}_4^{+}$.
